keyVerseText: But while he thought on these things, behold, the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a dream, saying, Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. conceived: Gr. begotten
rootMeaning: The Greek word κύριος (kýrios) derives from the root κῦρος (kŷros), which means supremacy or supreme authority. This etymological foundation highlights that the term is not merely a polite address but conveys the idea of one who possesses ultimate control and power. Unlike the English word 'lord,' which can sometimes be used loosely, κύριος inherently implies a status of sovereign authority and mastery.
usageInScripture: With 748 occurrences, κύριος is predominantly translated as 'Lord' or 'the Lord,' appearing over 450 times in these forms, which underscores its consistent use to denote someone with supreme authority. It is used both absolutely and with genitives to indicate ownership or control, often referring to God as the ultimate ruler. The term also applies respectfully to human masters or figures of authority, showing its range from divine to earthly lordship. This breadth reveals a word deeply embedded in expressing power, respect, and divine sovereignty throughout Scripture.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding κύριος as 'one who has supreme authority' is vital for grasping biblical teaching about God and Christ. It affirms that God is not a distant deity but the sovereign Lord over all creation, deserving of worship and obedience. In the New Testament, this term applied to Jesus highlights His divine lordship, reinforcing the Christian confession of His authority over life and death. Recognizing κύριος as a title of power and mastery helps believers submit to God's will and trust His control over all circumstances, anchoring faith in His ultimate supremacy.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 1:20, the phrase 'the angel of the Lord' uses κύριος to emphasize the divine authority behind the angel's message to Joseph. This assures Joseph that the conception of Jesus is by the Holy Spirit, underscoring God's sovereign plan in the incarnation. The word κύριος here reinforces that the message is not merely human advice but a command from the supreme Lord, inviting trust and obedience in the unfolding of God's redemptive work.
